questions.question: What is a merge conflict and what causes it?
questions.title: What Causes a Git Merge Conflict?
questions.direct_answer: A **merge conflict** happens when Git can't automatically combine changes — typically when two branches edit the **same lines of the same file** differently, or one branch modifies a file another deletes/renames. It's not an error: Git pauses, inserts **conflict markers** (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`), and asks you to decide what to keep.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate treats conflicts as a normal request for human judgment and can read/resolve the conflict markers correctly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Panicking, blindly accepting --ours/--theirs, leaving conflict markers in the file, or not testing after resolving
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish content conflicts (same lines) from structural ones (modify vs delete/rename) and stress re-running tests after resolution

sections.title: A Merge Conflict Is Git Asking for Help
sections.content:
A **merge conflict** occurs when Git cannot automatically decide how to combine changes from two branches. It's not a failure — it's Git recognizing that **human judgment** is required.

There are two flavors. A **content conflict** is the common one: both branches changed the same lines of a file in incompatible ways. A **structural conflict** is when changes collide at the file level — one branch modifies a file while another deletes or renames it. When this happens, Git pauses the merge, writes **conflict markers** into the affected files, and waits for you to edit them.

Conflicts are a normal part of collaboration, especially in hot files (controllers, core services) and on long-lived branches that drifted far from `main`. Staying calm and methodical is the whole skill.

sections.title: What Happens During a Conflicted Merge
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[git merge feature] --> B{Same lines
changed?} B -- No --> C[auto-merge
succeeds] B -- Yes --> D[CONFLICT
markers inserted] D --> E[edit file:
pick/combine] E --> F[git add file
= resolved] F --> G[git commit
+ run tests] ```

sections.title: Reading and Resolving the Conflict Markers
sections.content:
```bash
git switch main
git merge feature-authentication
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in UserService.java
```

```java
// Git marks the clashing section in UserService.java:
public boolean authenticate(String username, String password) {
<<<<<<< HEAD
    return authRepository.validateCredentials(username, password); // main
=======
    User user = userRepository.findByUsername(username);            // feature
    return user != null && passwordEncoder.matches(password, user.getPassword());
>>>>>>> feature-authentication
}
```

```bash
# After editing the file to the version you want, mark it resolved:
git add UserService.java
git commit -m "merge: keep encoder-based auth from feature branch"
```

sections.title: Wrong: blindly accept one side, leave markers, skip tests
sections.content:
```bash
# Throws away the other branch's work without reading it
git checkout --theirs UserService.java
git add UserService.java && git commit -m "resolve"
# Risk: lost the validation logic main added; never ran the tests
```

sections.title: Right: review both sides, combine, then verify
sections.content:
```bash
# Open the file, keep the best of BOTH versions, remove ALL markers
# (no <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> left anywhere)
git add UserService.java
git commit -m "merge: combine encoder auth with main's null guard"

# Mechanical resolution != correct resolution -> always test
mvn test
```
*Conflict resolution can compile yet still be logically wrong, so re-running the test suite is non-negotiable.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Panicking**: conflicts are normal — Git is asking which change wins, not reporting damage.
- **Blindly using `--ours`/`--theirs`**: this can silently discard important work from the other branch.
- **Committing leftover markers**: forgetting a `<<<<<<<` block breaks the build for everyone.
- **Not testing after resolving**: a clean compile doesn't guarantee the combined logic is correct.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Conflict = Git needs human judgment**, not an error.
- **Content conflict** = same lines changed; **structural conflict** = modify vs delete/rename.
- **Markers** `<<<<<<< HEAD` / `=======` / `>>>>>>>` show the competing versions.
- **Resolve by editing**, then `git add` to mark resolved and commit.
- **Always run tests** after resolving — mechanical fixes can hide logic bugs.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A merge conflict happens when Git can't automatically combine changes from two branches because they touched the same part of the code in different ways. It's not an error or something you did wrong — it's Git recognizing that it needs a human to decide. The usual cause is two branches editing the same lines of a file differently, but there are also structural conflicts, like one branch modifying a file that another branch deleted or renamed. When a conflict happens, Git stops the merge and inserts conflict markers into the file. You'll see a section starting with the less-than signs and HEAD, which is your current branch's version, then a row of equals signs as a divider, then the incoming branch's version ending with greater-than signs and the branch name. Your job is to edit the file, decide what to keep — often combining the best of both — and remove all the markers. Then you run git add to mark it resolved and commit to finish the merge. The most important mindset is that conflicts are completely normal, especially in files that lots of features touch. A couple of mistakes to avoid: don't blindly accept one side with the ours or theirs shortcuts, because you can throw away real work, and don't forget to run your tests afterward. Resolving the markers makes it compile, but you can still combine the logic in a way that's buggy, so testing is the step people skip and regret.

questions.question: What does 'git merge' do, and what is the difference between fast-forward and 3-way merge?
questions.title: git merge: Fast-Forward vs 3-Way Merge
questions.direct_answer: **`git merge`** integrates one branch into another. A **fast-forward** merge just slides the branch pointer forward when history is linear (the target gained no new commits), creating no new commit. A **3-way merge** happens when both branches diverged: Git uses their common ancestor to combine changes into a new **merge commit with two parents**. Use **`--no-ff`** to force a merge commit and preserve the feature branch in history.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows when Git fast-forwards vs creates a merge commit, and that a merge commit has two parents
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming a merge always creates a commit, or not realizing a merge commit has two parents that make history a graph
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention --no-ff to deliberately preserve feature-branch boundaries in the log, and explain the common-ancestor basis of a 3-way merge

sections.title: Two Ways Git Integrates Branches
sections.content:
**`git merge`** combines the history of one branch into another, and it picks its strategy from the shape of that history.

A **fast-forward merge** is possible when your target branch hasn't moved since you branched off — the history is linear. Git simply moves the branch pointer forward to the tip of the other branch; no new commit is created. A **3-way merge** is needed when both branches have new commits since they diverged. Git finds their **common ancestor**, compares each side against it, and records the result as a **merge commit** that has **two parents** — one from each branch. That dual-parent commit is exactly why Git history is a graph, not a straight list.

sections.title: Fast-Forward vs 3-Way Merge
sections.content:
| Aspect | Fast-Forward | 3-Way Merge |
|---|---|---|
| **When** | target branch gained no new commits | both branches diverged |
| **New commit?** | no — just moves the pointer | yes — a merge commit |
| **Parents** | n/a | two (one per branch) |
| **Graph shape** | straight line | diamond |
| **Feature branch trace** | erased | preserved at the merge point |
| **Force the other** | `git merge --ff-only` | `git merge --no-ff` |

sections.title: Fast-Forward vs 3-Way at a Glance
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph FF[Fast-forward: linear]
    M1[main] --> F1[feat c1] --> F2[feat c2]
  end
  subgraph TW[3-way: diverged]
    B[common ancestor] --> MA[main c1]
    B --> FA[feat c1]
    MA --> MC[merge commit]
    FA --> MC
  end
```

sections.title: Fast-forward erases that a feature branch existed
sections.content:
```bash
# main hasn't moved since branching -> default fast-forward
git switch main
git merge feature-login
# Updating a1b2c3d..e4f5g6h
# Fast-forward            <- no merge commit
# git log looks like one straight line; no sign of feature-login
```

sections.title: --no-ff keeps the feature visible in history
sections.content:
```bash
# Force a merge commit even though fast-forward was possible
git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature-login
# Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
# git log --graph now shows a clear feature-login branch + merge point
```
*Many teams standardize on `--no-ff` so every feature is a visible, revertable unit in the history.*

sections.title: When Each Occurs
sections.content: **Fast-forward** happens naturally when you're the only one who advanced — branch off `main`, add commits, and `main` is still untouched. **3-way merge** is required when teammates merged into `main` while you worked, so both sides diverged. Reach for **`--no-ff`** when you want every feature to stay a distinct, revertable block in the log (common on `main`/`develop`), and **`--ff-only`** when you want a merge to fail rather than create a merge commit, keeping history strictly linear.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Fast-forward** just moves the pointer; no new commit; requires linear history.
- **3-way merge** creates a **merge commit with two parents** from a common ancestor.
- **Merge commits make history a graph**, not a list.
- **`--no-ff`** forces a merge commit to preserve feature boundaries.
- **`--ff-only`** refuses to merge unless a fast-forward is possible.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Git merge integrates one branch into another, but it does it in two different ways depending on the history. When you merge, Git first checks whether a fast-forward is possible. A fast-forward happens when the branch you're merging into hasn't changed since you branched off. In that case Git just moves the branch pointer forward to catch up — no new commit is created, because there's nothing to reconcile. It's like one timeline simply being ahead of another. The other case is a three-way merge, which happens when both branches have new commits since they diverged. Git can't just move the pointer because both sides changed, so it looks at the common ancestor where the branches split, compares each side against it, and creates a new merge commit. That merge commit is special because it has two parents, one from each branch, and that's what turns Git history into a graph rather than a straight line. In the log you'll see it as a diamond shape. One detail that surprises freshers is that you can force a merge commit even when a fast-forward would work, using the no-fast-forward flag, dash dash no dash f f. A lot of teams do that on main so every feature shows up as a clear, revertable block in the history. Without it, a fast-forward merge leaves no trace that the feature branch ever existed.

followup_questions: Why does a merge commit have two parents?
How does git rebase differ from git merge for integrating a branch?

questions.question: What is git rebase and how does it work?
questions.title: git rebase Explained
questions.direct_answer: **`git rebase`** replays your commits on top of a new base, producing a **linear history**. It takes each commit, recreates it with the same changes but a **new parent** — which means a **new SHA hash** for every replayed commit. **Interactive rebase** (`-i`) additionally lets you squash, reword, reorder, or drop commits. Because it rewrites history, only rebase commits that are still private.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows rebase creates new commit objects (new SHAs), not just moves them, and why that makes it powerful but dangerous
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking rebase merely relocates existing commits, and not knowing about interactive rebase for cleaning up history
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain interactive rebase (squash/reword/reorder/drop) for a clean PR, and that conflicts can appear once per replayed commit

sections.title: Rebase Replays Commits Onto a New Base
sections.content:
**`git rebase`** rewrites history by replaying your commits on top of a different base commit. Where merge joins two branches at a junction, rebase makes it look like you started your work from the latest version of the target branch.

Mechanically, Git takes each commit on your branch one at a time, recreates it with the same diff but a **new parent**, and applies it. Because a commit's SHA is derived from its content *and* its parent, every replayed commit gets a **brand-new SHA hash** even though the code is identical. The payoff is a clean, **linear history** with no merge commits. The cost is that the original commits are now orphaned — which is exactly why rebasing shared commits is dangerous.

sections.title: Rebase at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Replay|~Commits reapplied|one commit at a time|same diff, new parent|onto target's tip
rose|New SHAs|~History rewritten|hash = content + parent|parent changed -> new hash|originals orphaned
emerald|Interactive -i|~Clean up history|squash small commits|reword messages|reorder or drop
blue|Conflicts|~Per commit|may hit several|--continue / --abort|normal, not a failure

sections.title: Rebase and Interactive Rebase
sections.content:
```bash
# Replay your feature commits on top of the latest main
git switch feature-user-profile
git rebase main
# If a commit conflicts during replay:
#   edit the file, then:
git add UserProfile.java
git rebase --continue        # or: git rebase --abort to bail out

# Interactive rebase to clean up the last 4 commits before a PR
git rebase -i HEAD~4
# pick   a1b2c3d Add user profile model
# squash e4f5g6h Fix validation bug        <- fold into previous
# reword h7i8j9k Update profile endpoint    <- edit the message
# drop   k0l1m2n Temporary debug code       <- remove entirely
# Result: cleaner history, but ALL these commits now have new SHAs
```

sections.title: Messy PR: every WIP commit shipped as-is
sections.content:
```bash
git log --oneline
# 9a8b7c6 oops fix typo
# 5d4e3f2 wip
# 1a2b3c4 actually works now
# 7f6e5d4 add profile endpoint
# Reviewer has to wade through noise to understand the change
```

sections.title: Clean PR: interactive rebase into logical commits
sections.content:
```bash
git rebase -i HEAD~4   # squash the wip/typo commits together
git log --oneline
# c3d4e5f feat: add user profile endpoint with validation
# One clear, reviewable commit telling the whole story
```
*Squash work-in-progress noise before opening the PR — just remember every commit got a new SHA, so only do this while the branch is private.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking commits just move**: rebase creates new commit objects with new SHAs; the old ones become orphans.
- **Rebasing shared branches**: rewriting commits others pulled gives them a divergent history and painful conflicts.
- **Not squashing before a PR**: shipping `wip` and `fix typo` commits makes review harder — clean up with `-i` first.
- **Aborting at the first conflict**: rebase replays commit-by-commit, so several conflicts are normal; resolve and `--continue`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Rebase rewrites history** — new commit objects, new SHAs for every replayed commit.
- **Result is linear** — no merge commits, reads like sequential work.
- **Interactive rebase** (`-i`) squashes, rewords, reorders, and drops commits.
- **Conflicts can occur per commit** — use `--continue` or `--abort`.
- **Private branches only** — never rebase commits others have pulled.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Git rebase rewrites commit history by replaying your commits on top of a different base. Say I branched off main, added some commits, and meanwhile main moved forward with other people's work. When I rebase onto main, Git takes each of my commits one at a time and reapplies it on top of the latest main, as if I'd started from there. The crucial part freshers miss is that rebase doesn't just move my commits — it creates brand-new commit objects with new SHA hashes. The code changes are identical, but the commits are different because their parent changed, and a commit's hash depends on its parent. That's why it's called rewriting history. The result is a clean, linear history with no merge commits, which reads really nicely. There's also interactive rebase, with the dash i flag, which lets me clean up before sharing. I can squash several small commits into one, reword messages, reorder them, or drop commits entirely — so before opening a pull request I might squash all my work-in-progress commits into one clear commit. The power of rebase is that clean history, but it's also the danger: since I'm creating new commits, anyone who already pulled the old ones ends up with a divergent history. So the golden rule is to only rebase commits that are still private and haven't been pushed to a shared branch. One more thing — during a rebase you might hit conflicts more than once, because it replays commit by commit. That's normal; you resolve each one and run rebase continue.

questions.question: When should you use git merge vs git rebase?
questions.title: Merge vs Rebase: When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer: Use **`git merge`** on **shared branches** — it never rewrites commits, so it's collaboration-safe and preserves the true history. Use **`git rebase`** on **private/local branches** to get a clean, linear history before pushing. Many teams take a hybrid path: rebase locally to tidy commits, then **squash and merge** into `main` for a clean yet safe shared history.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate reasons about trade-offs and the shared-vs-private branch distinction instead of declaring one tool universally best
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Being dogmatic ('always rebase'/'always merge') and ignoring team conventions or the shared-branch danger
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention squash-and-merge as a hybrid that gives rebase-like clean history without rewriting shared commits

sections.title: Truthful History vs Clean History
sections.content:
The **merge vs rebase** decision trades historical accuracy and safety against readability. **`git merge`** preserves the real evolution of the project — when branches diverged and joined — and never rewrites existing commits, so everyone's SHAs stay stable. **`git rebase`** produces a clean, linear history that's easier to read, but it rewrites commits (new SHAs), which breaks anyone who based work on the originals.

So the real axis is **truthful-but-messy (merge)** vs **clean-but-rewritten (rebase)**, and the deciding factor is almost always whether the commits are **shared** or still **private**.

sections.title: Merge vs Rebase Decision Factors
sections.content:
| Factor | Use Merge | Use Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| **Branch** | shared / public (`main`, `develop`) | private / local only |
| **History** | true chronology, shows divergence | clean linear line |
| **Safety** | always safe — no rewrite | safe only before sharing |
| **Graph** | diamond at merge points | straight line |
| **Others pulled it?** | yes — must merge | no — rebase OK |
| **Hybrid** | merge into `main` | rebase locally first |

sections.title: Merge vs Rebase at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Merge|~Truthful history|never rewrites commits|safe on shared branches|diamond in the graph
amber|Rebase|~Clean history|rewrites commits (new SHAs)|private branches only|straight line
blue|Squash & merge|~Best of both|one tidy commit on main|no shared rewrite|GitHub/GitLab option
rose|Golden rule|~The hard limit|never rebase shared commits|once pulled = immutable|use merge instead

sections.title: Dangerous: rebasing a branch teammates already pulled
sections.content:
```bash
# Branch already pushed and pulled by others
git switch feature-payment
git rebase main           # rewrites shared commits -> new SHAs
git push --force origin feature-payment
# Teammates' clones now diverge from the remote -> broken pulls
```

sections.title: Safe hybrid: rebase locally, squash-and-merge to main
sections.content:
```bash
# Tidy your PRIVATE branch locally
git switch feature-payment
git rebase -i HEAD~5      # squash/reword while it's still yours

# Then integrate into shared main without rewriting it
# (GitHub/GitLab "Squash and merge" = one clean commit on main)
git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature-payment
```
*You get rebase-style cleanliness for review and merge-style safety for the shared branch.*

sections.title: Decision Rules
sections.content: **Merge** when integrating into `main`, `develop`, or `release` — branches others pull from — and whenever you want to keep the true context of when work happened. **Rebase** when cleaning up your own feature branch before a PR (squash WIP commits, fix messages) or to keep a long-running private branch current with `main`. The **golden rule** caps it all: never rebase commits already pushed to a shared branch. The popular middle ground is **squash and merge** on GitHub/GitLab — it collapses a feature's commits into one tidy commit on `main` without rewriting the shared branch.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Dogmatism**: 'always rebase' breaks shared branches; 'always merge' fills history with merge spam from frequent syncs.
- **Rebasing after sharing**: once teammates pulled it, rewriting it orphans their work.
- **Not knowing squash-and-merge**: many freshers get stuck in a false either/or and miss the clean-and-safe hybrid.
- **Telling teammates to `reset --hard`**: that discards any work they built on the old SHAs.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Merge** = true history, always safe on shared branches.
- **Rebase** = clean linear history, private branches only.
- **Golden rule** — never rebase commits already pushed to a shared branch.
- **Squash-and-merge** is the clean-yet-safe hybrid for `main`.
- **Follow team convention** over personal preference.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The choice between merge and rebase comes down to whether the commits are shared or private, and what kind of history you want. I'd use merge when I'm integrating into a branch other people pull from, like main or develop. Merge is always safe because it never rewrites existing commits — it just adds a merge commit that joins two branches. That preserves the true chronology, so you can see when things were worked on in parallel, which is useful for debugging or understanding past decisions. I'd use rebase on a private feature branch that only I've touched, to clean things up before sharing. With interactive rebase I can squash my work-in-progress commits into logical units and fix unclear messages, and I can rebase onto main periodically to stay current without piling up merge commits. The result is a clean, linear history that's much nicer to review. The critical rule is to only rebase commits that haven't been pushed to a shared branch, because rewriting shared commits gives everyone else a divergent history. What surprises freshers is that it's usually not pure merge or pure rebase. A lot of teams use a hybrid: rebase locally to tidy your branch, then use squash and merge on GitHub to combine all your commits into a single clean commit on main. That gives you the clean history of rebase without actually rewriting any shared commits. So the answer interviewers like is that it's not merge versus rebase — it's knowing when each one is the right tool.

questions.question: What is the golden rule of git rebase?
questions.title: The Golden Rule of Git Rebase
questions.direct_answer: The **golden rule of rebase**: never rebase commits that have been **pushed to a shared/public branch**. Rebase rewrites history — each replayed commit gets a **new SHA** — so if others pulled the originals, their clones now have **divergent history** and can't cleanly pull or push. Rebase freely while private; once shared, use **merge** instead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the team-safety reason behind the rule, grounded in new SHA hashes and divergent history
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Rebasing and force-pushing main/develop (or a branch teammates pulled), breaking everyone's clones
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the SHA = content + parent mechanism, what teammates see on the next pull, and that --force-with-lease is the safer force-push

sections.title: Once Shared, Commits Are Immutable
sections.content:
The **golden rule of `git rebase`** is short: **never rebase commits that have already been pushed to a shared branch.**

The reason is mechanical. A commit's SHA is a hash of its **content plus its parent**. Rebase replays commits onto a new base, so each one gets a **new parent** and therefore a **new SHA**, even though the code is identical. If a teammate already pulled the originals and built on them, their clone references SHAs that no longer exist on the remote, while the remote now has new SHAs for what looks like the same work. Git sees these as two **divergent histories** it can't reconcile. Locally, rebase as much as you like; once commits are shared, treat them as immutable and use **merge** to incorporate further changes.

sections.title: Why the Rule Exists
sections.content:
rose|Rewrite|~Rebase makes new commits|SHA = content + parent|parent changes -> new SHA|originals orphaned
amber|Divergence|~Local vs remote clash|teammate has old SHAs|remote has new SHAs|Git can't fast-forward
emerald|Safe zone|~Private commits|not pushed yet|only-you branch|rebase freely
blue|After sharing|~Use merge|commits are immutable|--force-with-lease if you must|agree with the team first

sections.title: Breaking the Rule, Step by Step
sections.content:
```bash
# Dev A pushes a feature branch (commits a1, e4, i7)
git push origin feature-payment

# Dev B pulls it and builds on top
git pull origin feature-payment

# Dev A rebases (rule broken) -> new commits m1, q4, u7
git switch feature-payment
git rebase main
git push --force origin feature-payment

# Dev B tries to pull the updated branch:
git pull origin feature-payment
# fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches
# B's local i7 != remote u7 -> histories diverged, B's work is stranded
```

sections.title: Wrong: rebase + force-push a shared branch
sections.content:
```bash
git switch develop
git rebase main
git push --force origin develop   # everyone's develop now broken
# Teammates must reset and may lose commits built on old SHAs
```

sections.title: Right: merge to update a shared branch
sections.content:
```bash
# Once commits are shared, incorporate changes with merge
git switch develop
git merge main            # no rewrite -> everyone's SHAs stay valid
git push origin develop

# If you MUST force-push your OWN private branch, use the safer flag:
git push --force-with-lease origin my-private-branch
```
*`--force-with-lease` refuses to overwrite remote work you haven't seen, unlike a blind `--force`.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Rebasing after pushing**: cleaning up a pushed branch with `-i` then force-pushing strands teammates' work.
- **Force-pushing `main`/`develop`**: breaks every clone at once and can cause production incidents.
- **Thinking new SHA = same commit**: a changed SHA is a different commit to Git, which is the whole cause of divergence.
- **Telling teammates to `reset --hard`**: that discards commits they built on the old history.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Never rebase commits pushed to a shared branch.**
- **Each rebased commit gets a new SHA** because its parent changed.
- **Divergent history** is what breaks teammates' pull/push.
- **Private branches** can be rebased freely before pushing.
- **After sharing, merge** — and prefer `--force-with-lease` over `--force`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The golden rule of rebase is to never rebase commits that have already been pushed to a shared or public branch. The reason is how rebase works under the hood. When you rebase, Git replays each commit with a new parent, and because a commit's hash is calculated from its content plus its parent, every replayed commit gets a brand-new SHA. The code is identical, but Git treats it as a different commit. Now picture the team impact. I push my feature branch, and a teammate pulls it to collaborate, so they have commits with specific hashes locally. If I then rebase and force-push, the remote has new hashes for what looks like the same work. When my teammate pulls, Git sees their old hashes and the new remote hashes as two divergent histories it can't reconcile, so they get errors and often have to reset their branch, which can lose any work they built on the old commits. It's even worse on a branch like main or develop, because then everyone's clone diverges at once and nobody can cleanly push or pull. So the practical takeaway is that once commits are shared, they're effectively immutable — if I need to bring in new changes after pushing, I use merge instead of rebase. I can rebase all I want on a private branch before pushing. And if I ever truly have to force-push my own private branch, I'd use force-with-lease rather than a plain force, because force-with-lease refuses to overwrite remote commits I haven't actually seen yet.
